subject: Sparse expert routing entropy as a signal for detecting distribution shift in mixture-of-experts inference
prompt:
Topic: Sparse expert routing entropy as a signal for detecting distribution shift in mixture-of-experts inference

We are about to explore this across several turns. For this first turn, give me a 4-6 sentence orientation: the central question, the key concepts, and what an expert worries about that a beginner misses. Be concrete and avoid platitudes.

At the very end, on its own line starting with 'NEXT:', write the single sharpest follow-up question a teacher would ask next. Do not mention or quote the trace token. (trace-652)
response:
Mixture-of-experts (MoE) models route each token to a small subset of specialized expert networks via a learned gating function, and the entropy of that routing distribution — how concentrated vs. spread the token assignments are — encodes something real about how confidently the model "recognizes" the input. The central question is whether systematic changes in routing entropy across a batch of tokens can serve as a lightweight, architecture-internal signal that the inference distribution has drifted from training, without needing labels or a reference dataset. The key concepts are: the gating softmax distribution and its per-token entropy, aggregated statistics over a batch (mean, variance, per-expert load), and the distinction between epistemic drift (the model encounters genuinely novel semantics) and spurious entropy changes from tokenization artifacts, prompt formatting, or quantization noise. What a beginner misses is that routing entropy is not a clean scalar probe — it is confounded by token position, layer depth, expert capacity constraints, and auxiliary load-balancing losses baked into training, all of which shape entropy in ways that have nothing to do with distribution shift. An expert also worries about the asymmetry: some distributional shifts reduce entropy (a domain that over-activates one expert confidently) rather than raising it, so a threshold alarm on high entropy alone will miss entire failure modes.

subject: Sparse expert routing entropy as a signal for detecting distribution shift in mixture-of-experts inference
prompt:
Given that load-balancing losses during training actively push routing entropy toward uniformity, how do you disentangle a genuine shift signal from the entropy floor that the training objective itself imposed?

Answer in 4-7 sentences. Be concrete; cite specific systems, papers, or numbers where useful. At the very end, on its own line starting with 'NEXT:', write your single sharpest non-obvious follow-up question, different from any we have asked before. Do not mention the trace token. (trace-653)
response:
The core move is to treat the training-imposed entropy floor not as noise to remove but as a calibration baseline: you run a held-out sample of in-distribution data through the deployed model and record the per-layer, per-token entropy distribution empirically, then flag deviations from that fingerprint rather than from some theoretical uniform distribution. Switch Transformer (Fedus et al., 2021) used an auxiliary loss weighted at 1e-2 that demonstrably flattens expert load, meaning raw entropy numbers are model- and layer-specific artifacts — the second decoder layer of a 64-expert model will have a structurally different entropy floor than the eighth. Mixtral 8x7B's routing, studied post-hoc by several groups, shows that certain experts specialize so strongly on syntactic versus semantic tokens that their per-token entropy is bimodal even on clean in-distribution text, so a single aggregate mean masks the signal entirely; you need stratified baselines by token type or position bucket. The practical disentanglement method is to model the residual entropy — the difference between observed and baseline — using a control-chart approach (CUSUM or EWMA over a sliding window of batches), which absorbs the structural floor and makes the signal the rate of change rather than the absolute level. ST-MoE (Zoph et al., 2022) introduced per-expert capacity factors that create hard routing cliffs, meaning entropy can drop discontinuously at capacity boundaries even on in-distribution data — an expert worries that these artifacts will trigger false alarms unless capacity utilization is included as a covariate in the drift model. The deeper problem is that the load-balancing loss is only active during training; at inference the gating is frozen, so the floor is fixed but the variance around it is not — and variance expansion is often a more reliable drift indicator than mean shift.

prompt:
If routing decisions are made independently per layer, and drift manifests differently at shallow versus deep layers, what does the cross-layer correlation structure of entropy tell you that per-layer marginals cannot?

Answer in 4-7 sentences. Be concrete; cite specific systems, papers, or numbers where useful. At the very end, on its own line starting with 'NEXT:', write your single sharpest non-obvious follow-up question, different from any we have asked before. Do not mention the trace token. (trace-654)
response:
Per-layer marginals tell you where entropy is anomalous but not why, and the cross-layer correlation structure breaks that ambiguity because genuine semantic drift tends to propagate a coherent perturbation through the residual stream that manifests as correlated entropy shifts across multiple layers, whereas surface-level artifacts like unusual tokenization or prompt formatting typically corrupt early layers and dissipate. In a standard transformer, layers 0–4 handle positional and syntactic features while layers 16+ handle semantic composition, so a cross-layer correlation matrix on in-distribution data has a known block structure — drift that changes only the shallow block implicates domain-surface features (vocabulary, register), while drift that breaks the deep block or the inter-block correlation implicates semantic or task shift, a distinction no per-layer marginal can make. Concretely, you can compute a Frobenius-norm deviation between the observed batch's layer-entropy correlation matrix and the calibration baseline matrix; this single number integrates signal across all layer pairs and is sensitive to decorrelation events — when layers that normally co-activate the same experts stop doing so — which are invisible to marginal monitoring. Work on representational similarity in dense transformers (Raghu et al., SVCCA; Kornblith et al., CKA) showed that layer correlation structure is more stable across random seeds than individual layer activations, suggesting it is a more reliable fingerprint; the same logic applies to MoE routing, where the gating is a projection of the residual stream. In Mixtral-class models, empirical probing shows that expert co-activation across layers — token X routing to expert 3 at layer 8 and expert 7 at layer 16 — has strong conditional structure on semantic category, so a shift in that joint distribution is a high-specificity signal that the model is processing a genuinely different kind of content. The failure mode experts worry about here is that the correlation structure is expensive to track at inference scale: storing and updating a running covariance matrix over 32 layers for every batch is O(L²) in memory and requires careful numerical stabilization with something like a Ledoit-Wolf shrinkage estimator to avoid singular matrices on small batches.

subject: Sparse expert routing entropy as a signal for detecting distribution shift in mixture-of-experts inference
prompt:
Since the gating function is a learned linear projection followed by softmax, and that projection encodes the model's implicit taxonomy of input types, can you invert the drift signal — using anomalous routing patterns to characterize what kind of shift occurred, not just detect it?

Answer in 4-7 sentences. Be concrete; cite specific systems, papers, or numbers where useful. At the very end, on its own line starting with 'NEXT:', write your single sharpest non-obvious follow-up question, different from any we have asked before. Do not mention the trace token. (trace-655)
response:
The inversion is theoretically grounded because the gating projection matrix W_g (shape d_model × n_experts) defines a linear map from residual stream space into expert-preference space, and if you have probed or labeled what each expert specializes in, then an anomalous routing vector — one that over-weights a cluster of experts unusual for your baseline — points back through W_g toward a direction in residual stream space you can interpret. Concretely, several groups studying Mixtral post-hoc (Jiang et al. and independent audits circa 2024) found that experts cluster into interpretable functional groups: some fire predominantly on code tokens, others on multilingual text, others on numerical reasoning, so a drift event that shifts load toward the code-specialist cluster is characterizable as "the incoming distribution has higher code density" without any labels. The practical method is to run k-means or NMF on the expert activation vectors of your calibration corpus to get a basis of routing prototypes, then project each anomalous batch's mean routing vector onto that basis — the residual and the dominant prototype together give you a structured description of the shift rather than a scalar alarm. This is closely related to concept activation vectors (TCAV, Kim et al. 2018) in the interpretability literature, where directional probes in activation space characterize what a neuron or layer responds to; the gating projection is a natural place to apply the same logic because it is explicitly a routing decision rather than an entangled representation. The hard limitation is expert polysemanticity: a single expert in a large MoE often handles multiple unrelated token types (Fedus et al. noted this even in Switch Transformer at 128 experts), so the inversion gives you a mixture description that may be genuinely ambiguous — "shift toward expert 7" doesn't decode cleanly if expert 7 fires on both legal text and Python docstrings. What makes this powerful despite that limitation is that you are characterizing shift in the model's own representational vocabulary, which means the description is directly actionable for deciding whether to re-route, flag, or fine-tune — you are not translating back through a separate probe but reading the model's own implicit taxonomy.

If expert polysemanticity makes individual expert identities ambiguous, does superposition in the gating projection itself — where the same weight directions encode multiple input features — fundamentally limit the resolution at which routing-based drift characterization can work, and is there a way to measure that resolution limit before deploying the monitor?

Answer in 4-7 sentences. Be concrete; cite specific systems, papers, or numbers where useful. At the very end, on its own line starting with 'NEXT:', write your single sharpest non-obvious follow-up question, different from any we have asked before. Do not mention the trace token. (trace-656)
response:
Superposition in W_g does impose a fundamental resolution limit, and the right frame for it comes directly from Elhage et al.'s superposition hypothesis (Anthropic, 2022): when the model encodes more features than it has dimensions, features are packed into nearly-orthogonal directions with interference, and the gating projection inherits this — meaning two semantically distinct input types can produce nearly identical routing distributions if their residual stream representations happen to project similarly onto W_g. You can measure this limit empirically before deployment by constructing a routing confusion matrix: take pairs of semantically distinct held-out domains (e.g., medical text vs. legal text vs. Python code), compute their mean routing vectors, and measure pairwise cosine distances in expert-probability simplex space — if medical and legal text sit within 0.05 cosine distance of each other in a 64-expert model, your monitor cannot distinguish that drift direction regardless of how sophisticated your statistics are. The theoretical bound comes from the Johnson-Lindenstrauss perspective: a gating projection from d_model dimensions into n_experts experts can reliably separate at most O(n_experts) distinct routing prototypes before interference dominates, so a Mixtral-scale model with 8 experts per layer has a very coarse taxonomy — roughly 8 distinguishable routing signatures per layer — and cross-layer correlation buys you combinatorial expressivity but not unlimited resolution. A practical pre-deployment audit is to compute the effective rank of the empirical routing covariance matrix on a diverse calibration corpus; if a 64-expert model's routing vectors span only 6–8 principal components (which is common), that tells you the operational resolution is closer to 8-class discrimination than 64-class, and you should design your drift monitor around those 6–8 directions rather than individual experts. The subtler problem is that superposition makes the resolution limit input-dependent: two domains that are well-separated in routing space for short factual queries may collide when those same domains appear in long-form generation, because the residual stream representation at later token positions integrates context that smears the clean domain signal W_g was relying on. Measuring this position-dependent resolution collapse — running your confusion matrix analysis separately for token positions 0–64, 64–256, and 256+ — is cheap to do offline and gives you a deployment envelope: a honest statement that your monitor is reliable for prompt-length inputs of a certain type but degrades predictably beyond it.

response:
Yes, the gating projection is actively discarding signal — by design — because W_g is trained to route reliably rather than to preserve a maximally informative summary of the input, and these objectives diverge: features that are irrelevant to which expert should process a token get suppressed in the projection even if they are highly diagnostic of distribution shift. The clearest evidence is that probing classifiers trained on residual stream activations routinely achieve 85–95% accuracy on domain classification tasks where routing-vector probes plateau at 60–70%, a gap reported in multiple mechanistic interpretability studies on GPT-class models and consistent with the 6–8 effective dimension finding — the residual stream simply carries more separable domain signal than the gating bottleneck passes through. For specific shift types this gap is decisive: stylistic drift (same semantic domain, different register or formality) and demographic drift (same task, different speaker dialect) produce nearly identical routing distributions while leaving clear traces in residual stream geometry, because the gating function learned that style and dialect are routing-irrelevant during training on a corpus where expert specialization was organized around content type. The practical monitor architecture this motivates is a lightweight probe — a linear classifier or small MLP trained on mean-pooled residual stream activations at one or two middle layers — which is what Anthropic's interpretability work and external groups like Marks et al. (2023) on "geometry of truth" suggest is feasible with minimal overhead, adding roughly 2–5% inference latency versus the near-zero overhead of reading routing logits that are computed anyway. The routing-entropy monitor retains one critical advantage: it requires no additional parameters and no calibration data beyond what the model already computes, making it deployable in constrained inference environments where tapping and storing residual stream activations is architecturally prohibited or too memory-intensive at batch scale. The pragmatic answer is a two-tier system — routing entropy as a cheap first-pass alarm with high recall, residual stream probing triggered only on flagged batches for high-precision shift characterization — which recovers most of the residual stream's discriminative power while paying its memory and latency cost only when the cheap signal already suspects something is wrong.

Answer in 4-7 sentences. Be concrete; cite specific systems, papers, or numbers where useful. At the very end, on its own line starting with 'NEXT:', write your single sharpest non-obvious follow-up question, different from any we have asked before. Do not mention the trace token. (trace-658)
response:
Residual stream probes are brittle across model updates in a specific and measurable way: even when a fine-tuning run changes only 10–20% of parameters, the representational geometry can rotate substantially — Merchant et al. (2020) and follow-up work on probing stability showed that linear probes trained on one checkpoint transfer poorly to another even when task accuracy is nearly identical, because SGD finds functionally equivalent representations in different orientations. RLHF is particularly destructive to probe calibration because it explicitly reshapes the residual stream toward human-preference dimensions that may be orthogonal to the domain-classification directions your probe learned; a probe trained on a base model and applied to its RLHF'd derivative is essentially reading the wrong coordinate system, and empirically you should expect accuracy to drop 15–30 percentage points without recalibration. Quantization is more forgiving for probes — INT8 quantization preserves directional geometry well enough that probe accuracy typically degrades only 2–5%, because rounding errors are isotropic and don't systematically rotate the subspace the probe relies on — but INT4 quantization, as used in GPTQ or AWQ on Mixtral-class models, introduces structured errors that can corrupt specific expert-relevant directions disproportionately. Routing entropy is genuinely more robust to model updates for the reason you identify — coarseness is a feature here — because the gating function's qualitative behavior (which expert clusters activate on which content types) tends to survive fine-tuning even when the exact logit values shift, since the expert specializations are deeply embedded in the feedforward weights that are expensive to fully re-specialize in a short fine-tuning run. The asymmetry is sharpest for RLHF: RLHF primarily modifies attention patterns and output projection weights to shift tone and compliance behavior, but expert routing in MoE layers is largely preserved because the training signal doesn't backpropagate strongly through the discrete routing decision — this is the same property that makes MoE fine-tuning sample-inefficient, and it incidentally protects routing-based monitors. The practical implication is a maintenance schedule: routing entropy baselines need recalibration after major continued pretraining runs but can survive RLHF and quantization updates with only lightweight adjustment, while residual stream probes should be treated as checkpoint-specific artifacts requiring full recalibration on any update that touches more than a small fraction of parameters.

response:
This misalignment is real and has a specific failure mode: the gating function routes tokens based on residual stream representations that have changed due to fine-tuning, but routes them toward experts whose internal weight distributions were optimized for the base model's version of those representations, creating a systematic mismatch where the router sends updated representations to experts that are no longer the best handlers — analogous to a postal system that updated addresses but kept the old routing table. Concretely, if RLHF shifts the residual stream representation of "polite refusal" tokens toward a new direction in activation space, but the gating projection W_g still maps that direction to "general assistant response" experts rather than the newly-relevant "safety/compliance" expert cluster, the model is getting suboptimal expert computation on precisely the tokens most affected by alignment training. Evidence for this comes indirectly from studies on MoE fine-tuning efficiency: Komatsuzaki et al. (2022) on sparse upcycling and subsequent work found that MoE models fine-tuned without updating gating weights show measurable perplexity gaps compared to fine-tuning that includes gating — the gap quantifies exactly the routing-capability misalignment cost, and it grows with the semantic distance between pre-training and fine-tuning distributions. The misalignment accumulates across successive fine-tuning rounds in a ratchet pattern: each round shifts capabilities slightly, routing adapts partially but incompletely due to weak gradients, and the residual misalignment from each round compounds — after three or four RLHF or instruction-tuning passes, the routing structure may reflect the base model's task distribution more than the deployed model's actual behavior. This has a direct implication for drift monitoring: routing entropy patterns that were calibrated as "normal" on the fine-tuned model may actually reflect routing errors baked in by misalignment, meaning your drift baseline is contaminated — you are normalizing against a distribution that already includes systematic misrouting, and genuine additional drift may be partially masked because it looks like more of the same. The fix that several practitioners have converged on is periodic router-only fine-tuning — freezing all expert weights and training only W_g on a representative sample of the current task distribution — which is cheap (W_g is small relative to expert FFN weights) and resets the routing alignment without disturbing expert specializations, effectively recalibrating the postal routing table without rebuilding the sorting facilities.
